sources.title: Judge tosses Trump lawsuit against WSJ, Murdoch over Epstein story
sources.text:
A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein,
Why it matters: It's the second time this year courts have blocked Trump's efforts to sue the paper over stories about his relationship with the disgraced financier.
Driving the news: Judge Darrin Gayles of the southern district of Florida issued the 20-page ruling Saturday afternoon, finding that Trump failed to prove the paper acted with "actual malice" by reporting on his links to Epstein.
Zoom out: Trump first filed suit against the paper and Murdoch in July 2025, seeking $20 billion in damages.
What they're saying: "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false," Gayles wrote.
For the record: "President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," a spokesman for his legal team said in a statement.
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.
Sara Fischer contributed.

sources.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
sources.text:
- Published
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.
This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.
Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.
Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.
The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.
Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.
In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.
The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".
The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.
Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.
Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.
North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.
In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.
TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.
Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.
Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.
In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

sources.title: Anthropic Blocks AI Game Clones in Claude Opus Update
sources.text:
Anthropic has issued an update for Claude that puts a stop to the AI-generated game clones that have filled platforms like Steam.
The term 'AI slop' is something we've heard a lot in the past few years, but it became especially prevalent in the gaming community after Valve launched Steam Next Fest earlier this month. PC users quickly launched complaints that their feeds had been filled with low-effort clones not only of pre-existing games but even some titles that had only just released their own demos.
As players trudged through the slop, developers faced a reality that threw months or even years of hard work into jeopardy. Some, including Drunken Goddess Reflux developer Alliance Arts and Who You, even took action by canceling their Steam demo plans in favor of private playtests. It's a situation that rapidly spun out of control, prompting a response from Valve itself as it said it would be "thinking about how to solve this problem."
ANTHROPIC IS CRACKING DOWN ON VIDEO GAME REWRITES 🚨
Claude Code picked up a new rule around Oct 27, sent from Anthropic’s servers under a flag called "tengu_heron_brook". There’s no setting to turn it off.
The full rule: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”
Is this the end of game rewrites, modding and everything in between?
— chasm (@chasmmmmmmmmmmm) October 30, 2026
As reported by Game Developer, X/Twitter user Chasm was one of the first to share evidence of tech company Anthropic taking action against video game copycats. Based on their findings, Claude, the company's AI assistant, recently received an update featuring a new rule. The full rule can be read below:
"Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."
When reached for comment by Game Developer, Anthropic pointed to a post shared by Addy Osmani, a member of its technical staff. Osmani's explanation can be read below:
"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."
Whether there was a specific event or reason that prompted Anthropic to make these changes is unclear.
Game developers and game enjoyers will no doubt find comfort in Anthropic's changes, though it's worth noting that how impactful any of this will be remains to be seen. At the very least, those who use Claude to rip ideas directly from those who used their minds and time to bring them to life should have a tougher time trying to profit off of the work of others.
The industry is struggling to come to grips with artificial intelligence. Some, such as Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, have insisted that Valve should stray from asking developers to disclose games utilizing generative AI materials. Others, including Super Smash Bros. mastermind Masahiro Sakurai, have compared AI-generated games to "low-quality goods." The developers behind VRChat, meanwhile, recently came under fire for how they are handling AI content.

sources.title: Anthropic takes steps to block Claude from reverse-engineering video games
sources.text:
According to reporting from Tom's Hardware, Anthropic's Claude AI has quietly started restricting the kinds of work it will do, including modding, decompiling, or reverse-engineering video game code. And though there has as yet been no official announcement about why, the reason is still pretty obvious.
The video game community has been in the news a lot lately, first because of the GTA6 leaks that went mega-viral and spurred Take-Two Interactive into getting subpoenas against both Microsoft and Discord in the hopes of finding the responsible parties, and next because the hacking and modding community discovered how much easier AI makes their job.
First, game decompilers went into overdrive, playing around with the source code of multiple different video games to, for example, put Nintendo's Mario inside the dark gothic world of Elden Ring, or import Spider-Man into the Batman: Arkham City game, seamlessly blending the mechanics of one character into the world of another. Next came the ports: World of Warcraft, Call of Duty, and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City made playable in a browser, without the original developers or copyright owners having any say in the matter.
These initial modifications and ports were already giving gaming companies nightmares, teasing a future without system gatekeeping, but things really got out of hand with the PlayStation 5 jailbreak, which resulted in everything from backward compatibility with older-gen PlayStation games to cross-platform play, with users figuring out how to run Xbox-exclusive titles like Halo 2 and acclaimed Nintendo titles like Zelda: Breath of the Wild on a jailbroken PS5.
Given the potential number of lawsuits these jailbreaks could cause, and the astronomically high nature of the monetary damages, it's no surprise that AI companies are scrambling to shut down or severely restrict these pathways, but it's also deeply ironic. As Tom's Hardware reporter Bruno Ferreira notes, this sudden concern for copyright "highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement."
There's also the ugly truth that, if one company makes a gesture toward respecting copyright law or basic ethics, the bad actors can find another LLM that won't (or hasn't yet) taken the same precautions, creating a kind of AI arms race driven by perverse incentives: the least ethical AI might be poised to become the most popular.

sources.text:
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.
Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars.
Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.
Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets.
The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”
Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.
Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.
In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.”
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

What appears to be gameplay footage from an unannounced Persona 1 remake has leaked online.
A little less than two minutes of video depicting what looks a lot like a modern version of Sega and Atlus' original Persona game was first published on Reddit before being spread around various social media platforms today. The developers behind the RPG franchise have broached the topic of remakes for early installments in the past but never confirmed work was underway, meaning this could be our first look at the series' next remake.
The original post says the footage is tied to a Persona: Be Your True Mind remake. In the age of AI-generated fakes, you can never be too skeptical about things like this, but fans generally seem to be under the impression that the footage is authentic. We won't share it here, but you don't have to look too hard on places like X/Twitter or YouTube to see what everyone's talking about.
Yea that Persona 1 remake leaked footage gotta be 100% real. I refuse to believe someone would do that much work to make a fake leak.

Aside from the music, effects, and art, which all fall right in line with much of the studio's recent work, the video on display is much longer and more detailed than any fake leak would typically be. The smoking gun for many, though, is the character animations.
It's specifically Eriko that people are calling out, as she seems to share a summoning animation with Persona 4 Revival's version of Yukiko. Atlus' Persona 4 remake, of course, won't be out until February 18, 2027. There's also the issue of the appearance of Persona 2 protagonist Tatsuya, who seems to be standing in for what may be an unfinished character model.

There is always the chance this could be an elaborate fake, with some of these odd details serving as evidence for that argument. On the other hand, it's possible placeholder assets and familiar animations are here specifically because the alleged Persona 1 remake is still very much in development.
Persona 1 leak looks credible, not sure why people are reporting Tatsuya is replacing Masao, that's just complete bogus.
This is most likely an internal investor pitch for remakes of Persona 1 and 2, and not actually Persona 1.
There are Persona 4 Revival animations in the gameplay footage, which definitely helps the case of it being real.

That sure is a persona 1 remake trailer. Why is tatsuya there

We don't know when this footage would have been captured, even if it does turn out to be real. That means this could be from yesterday or years ago, with some speculating that the video we've seen today is little more than a proof-of-concept or pitch video.

sources.title: This Rosy Stone Spotted in the Sahara Turned Out to Be a 4.1-Billion-Year-Old Meteorite From Mars, One of the Oldest Ever Found
sources.text:
In 2022, a strange, rosy stone was discovered in the Sahara Desert. Now, scientists have found that the nearly two-pound object is a Martian meteorite made of rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. The findings, published October 29 in the journal Science, mean it’s one of the oldest known samples of Mars and can help researchers better understand what the Red Planet was like in its youth.
“We’re holding a piece of a rock that’s dated even before the oldest Earth rock—a piece of Mars that’s so ancient, it existed when life had just started on Earth,” study co-author Yang Liu, a geologist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, tells Scientific American’s Mary Randolph.
Scientists know of more than 400 Martian meteorites. These pieces were ejected from the Red Planet when impactors hit the celestial body. The debris was flung toward Earth, passed through our atmosphere without completely burning up and then landed on the planet’s surface. Previously, only two meteorites provided snapshots of a young Mars, which formed around 4.5 billion years ago: Allan Hills 84001, dated at 4.1 billion years old, and Northwest Africa 7034, which contains fragments dated at more than 4.3 billion years old.
To figure out the age of the Sahara meteorite, called Teghaza 001, Liu and colleagues looked at the zircon crystals within it, which contain the element uranium. Researchers often date rocks by examining the decay of uranium into lead. The team also analyzed different forms of the elements rubidium and strontium in the meteorite, which yielded a similar age estimate.
Teghaza 001’s age isn’t its only special feature. Unlike the other two oldest known Martian meteorites, the rosy space rock’s composition of volcanic minerals reveals that the fragment was originally a bunch of magma. It cooled and hardened into part of Mars’ outermost layer, the crust, and was further transformed by underground water, according to chemical analyses. This evidence of the meteorite’s past interactions with water joins a growing body of research indicating that Mars—now a dry, dusty world—was once a much wetter place.
“When you add a third sample, and its geochemistry is really unique compared to the other samples that we have, it lets us see a different part of Mars’ ancient history in terms of what the mantle looked like and what the different mantle sources were on Mars,” says study co-author Alicia Cruz-Uribe, a geochemist at the University of Maine, in a statement.
Did you know? Mission to a Martian moon
Earlier this month, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency launched a spacecraft to recover samples from Phobos, one of Mars’ moons. Because Phobos may have gotten sprayed with Martian dust when impactors hit the Red Planet, researchers hope the samples contain bits of Mars.
Mars’ past watery environment is one reason that researchers think the planet could have hosted life long ago, since all known organisms need water.

However, they “do not directly answer the question of whether there was life on Mars.”

sources.title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution
sources.text:
SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday.
The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis.
The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years.
The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026.
The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby."
(SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.)
The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit.
Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional.
The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed."
The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

sources.title: SpaceX Starship Flight 15: Launch date, objectives, and what to expect
sources.text:
SpaceX is targeting November 2026 for the 15th integrated flight test of its Starship rocket, with the mission expected to attempt a major milestone: catching the spacecraft’s upper stage at its launch tower after returning from space.
The company is also preparing to recover the Super Heavy booster, potentially bringing both stages of its massive launch system back to the launch site.
As of October 28, SpaceX has not announced an official launch date. However, preparations are progressing at Starbase in South Texas, where the company is testing the vehicles assigned to the mission.
The flight will build on September’s Flight 14, which reached orbit and deployed 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.
SpaceX is currently targeting November, although the launch date will depend on testing, vehicle readiness, and regulatory approval.
On October 25, the company conducted a full-duration static-fire test of Super Heavy Booster 22, igniting all 33 Raptor engines for about 15 seconds. The test allows engineers to assess engine and vehicle systems while the booster remains secured to the ground.
According to Space.com, the booster will fly with Starship upper stage Ship 42. The spacecraft has completed its own engine test and is undergoing final systems checks ahead of the launch.
The Federal Aviation Administration’s launch authorization is another factor. SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell said during an October earnings call that the company expected its license for Flight 15 to cover return-to-launch-site operations and tower catches for both stages, as reported by Ars Technica.
The primary objective is to demonstrate the recovery of both components of the Starship launch system. After liftoff, Super Heavy provides the initial thrust needed to propel Starship toward orbit before separating from the upper stage. SpaceX plans to guide the booster back to Starbase, where mechanical arms mounted on the launch tower, nicknamed “chopsticks,” will attempt to catch it.
SpaceX has already demonstrated booster catches on earlier flights. Flight 15, however, is expected to use the upgraded Booster 22 and attempt the recover both stages in the same mission.
The more ambitious objective is to catch Ship 42 after its orbital flight. Starship will need to reenter the atmosphere, withstand intense heating, and maneuver toward the launch tower for a controlled capture. The spacecraft has previously performed controlled ocean splashdowns, but a tower catch would be a significant step toward making the entire system reusable.
Recovering both stages could eventually reduce refurbishment requirements and the cost of launching payloads. However, a successful catch alone would not prove that Starship can be rapidly inspected, refurbished, and reflown.
Flight 15 also follows a significant milestone from the previous mission. On September 28, Flight 14 reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, demonstrating Starship’s ability to carry operational payloads. SpaceX has not officially confirmed Flight 15’s payload, though it has discussed another Starlink deployment as a possibility. The program also has implications for NASA’s Artemis lunar exploration campaign.

sources.title: How big and powerful is SpaceX's Starship rocket?
sources.text:
How big and powerful is SpaceX's Starship rocket?
Bigger isn't always better, but when it comes to space exploration, it just might be.
With both stages stacked, the current SpaceX Starship launch vehicle stands at 407 feet. It's taller than the tallest known living tree, Hyperion, and one-third taller than the Statue of Liberty (pedestal included). It's the tallest rocket ever flown and the most powerful, with 18.1 million pounds-force of liftoff thrust. During its first full-stack launch in April 2023, the booster's exhaust shattered the concrete launch pad, excavating the earth beneath and flinging debris across 385 acres. That booster was rated at 16.7 million pounds of thrust, slightly less than the one on the September 28, 2026, launch.
Keep in mind that this height covers the complete two-stage vehicle. The bottom section, known as Super Heavy, is the 236.2-foot booster that provides the initial push from the launch pad. Above it sits the 170.6-foot Starship spacecraft. While it's immense in size and power, its dimensions serve a greater purpose than impressions alone. SpaceX designed the system to transport huge payloads and eventually carry people and cargo beyond Earth orbit. SpaceX also intends to recover and reuse both stages.
How much power does Starship produce?
The Super Heavy booster packs 33 Raptor engines, which burn liquid methane and liquid oxygen to generate 18.1 million pounds-force of booster thrust. For an interesting perspective, NASA's Space Launch System produces 8.8 million to 9.4 million pounds of max thrust. Once Super Heavy separates, Starship will go on, powered by three regular Raptor engines and three Raptor Vacuum engines designed to operate in space. SpaceX lists the upper stage's thrust at roughly 3.5 million pounds-force. Only the booster figure represents liftoff thrust.
The rocket's immense power has to do more than fight gravity to lift heavy payloads. Super Heavy has a listed propellant capacity of 3,650 metric tons, and Starship holds an additional 1,600 metric tons. That's 5,250 metric tons on top of everything else. With all of that weight, the world's most powerful rocket still depends on staging, very efficient engines and a considerable degree of careful pre-launch planning.
Can Starship go to the Moon without refueling?
Despite all of today's technological advancements, Starship will still have to refuel in Earth orbit, at least as far as NASA's planned lunar-landing missions are concerned. The SpaceX lunar lander burns through a significant portion of its propellant just to reach orbit and will have to refuel.
SpaceX and NASA's game plan includes several specialized vehicles, including a propellant depot that launches first, followed by tanker Starships that deliver fuel. The lunar lander launches last, docks with the depot and takes on propellant.
All of this takes place before the crew launches aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft (part of the Artemis program), after which they will meet with the prepositioned Starship lander in Earth orbit before Starship pushes both spacecraft to lunar orbit. The Starship lander will then carry two crew members to the Moon's surface and back. Transporting and storing extremely cold propellants in space is a herculean technical challenge, so planned stages, refueling and a complicated support system are necessary to pull everything off successfully.

sources.title: What is EIP-7702? The Ethereum Upgrade Behind the $6.4B Binance Hack
sources.text:
In brief
- EIP-7702 is an Ethereum upgrade, activated in May 2025, that lets standard wallets temporarily take on the abilities of smart contracts.
- It enables batched transactions, gas sponsorship and limited-permission keys, but delegated code gets full access to the wallet's funds.
- An attacker used EIP-7702 in October 2026 to drain a Binance hot wallet during a $6.4 billion hack that analysts attributed to North Korea.
Ethereum has two kinds of accounts. Externally owned accounts (EOAs), the standard wallets most people use, are controlled by a private key and can do little more than send transactions. Smart contract accounts can run code, enabling features like spending limits, account recovery and paying fees in tokens other than ETH, but most users never moved to them.
EIP-7702 is an attempt to bridge that gap. Instead of asking users to migrate to new wallets, it lets existing EOAs borrow the code of a smart contract while keeping their address and funds.
This guide explains what EIP-7702 is, how it works, why developers wanted it, and how attackers used it in the largest crypto theft on record.
What is EIP-7702?
EIP-7702, titled "Set Code for EOAs," is an Ethereum Improvement Proposal written in May 2024 by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin and developers Sam Wilson, Ansgar Dietrichs and lightclient, according to the official specification.
It was one of the headline changes in Pectra, a major Ethereum upgrade that went live on May 7, 2025.
"EIP-7702 lays the foundation we've needed for a long time," Ethereum core developer Preston Van Loon told Decrypt at the time. "While full abstraction won't be immediately available to end users with Pectra, this upgrade gives Ethereum the infrastructure to support it moving forward."
EIP-7702 is a change to Ethereum's core protocol, not a token or a separate blockchain, so there is nothing to buy.
How does EIP-7702 work?
EIP-7702 adds a new type of Ethereum transaction, the "set code transaction." It carries a list of authorizations, each signed with the private key of the account being upgraded, that names the address of a smart contract the account wants to use.
Once the transaction is processed, the account stores a small pointer, called a delegation indicator, to that contract. From then on, whenever anyone calls the account, Ethereum runs the contract's code as if it belonged to the account, with full access to its funds.
The delegation lasts until the account owner signs a new authorization, either pointing to a different contract or clearing the pointer to restore a plain EOA.
Did you know?
EIP-7702 marks delegated accounts using the byte 0xef, a code value that was banned in earlier upgrades so it could be reserved for special purposes like this.
What's so special about EIP-7702?
The specification names three main features it was designed to deliver:
- Batching: combining several actions, such as approving a token and then swapping it, into a single transaction.
- Sponsorship: letting another account, such as an app, pay transaction fees on a user's behalf, with the user possibly reimbursing it in another token.
- Privilege de-escalation: creating sub-keys with limited permissions, such as spending only a certain token or only 1% of a balance per day.

sources.title: North Korean hackers pull off a $6.3 billion crypto heist in one of the biggest thefts so far
sources.text:
North Korean hackers have stolen a staggering $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. On October 29 the attack reportedly drained funds across 10 different blockchains in roughly 20 minutes. TRM attributes the operation to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group.
How did hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance?
On Ethereum, the hackers exploited a mechanism involving Ethereum’s EIP-7702 standard to hijack a Binance hot wallet and turn it into a contract they fully controlled. They used one of 50 pre prepared authorizations that happened to match the wallet’s transaction count.
On the other nine blockchains, they simply moved funds using ordinary signed transfers. TRM believes Binance’s wallet signing system itself was likely compromised, though Binance has not confirmed exactly how it happened.
The group reportedly started preparing at least 36 hours earlier, running test transactions and funding an operator wallet through small withdrawals from Tornado Cash. TRM Labs says the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor is also tied to last year’s $1.5 billion Bybit hack, making this one about four times bigger.
The stolen assets included Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, and stablecoins. Binance confirmed the security incident and temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks. It said user funds were safe, although the investigation is ongoing.
How much of the stolen cryptocurrency has been recovered?
The good news is that companies like Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial managed to freeze about $2.7 billion of the stolen funds pretty quickly. The bad news is that the hackers still hold around $2.4 billion worth of assets, including over 420,000 ETH and more than 18,000 bitcoin, sitting safely outside anyone’s reach.
Hackers have already started laundering some of it, selling tokens likely to get frozen to market makers at a discount and routing funds through multiple wallets to cover their tracks. TRM expects the next stage to involve bridges and swap services, so this story is far from over.
The incident highlights how dangerous compromised transaction-signing systems can be for cryptocurrency exchanges. Even with billions frozen, recovering the remaining funds could prove difficult.

Binance heist: How were cryptocurrency billions stolen?
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, estimates that assets worth $6.3 billion were impacted by a hacking attack against the trading platform.
But how was such a theft possible, and what does it reveal about the security of cryptocurrencies? AFP takes a look.
Is Binance reliable?
Binance, the world's largest platform by digital currency trading volume, claims to have 335 million users.
That compares to the reported 741 million cryptocurrency owners worldwide cited by Crypto.com.
However, Binance has faced its fair share of scandals. Its former CEO, Changpeng Zhao, was convicted in the United States in 2024 for violating anti-money laundering laws, though he was later pardoned by President Donald Trump.
It has faced further U.S. legal troubles, including being accused of selling assets that qualify as unregistered securities.
In France, Binance is suspected of having failed to meet its obligations regarding the oversight of client funds.
Having failed to obtain authorization under the European Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) regulation, Binance recently announced a partial suspension of its operations within the European Union.
A secure technology?
Cryptocurrencies are based on a technology called blockchain, a digital ledger that records transactions and is designed to make falsification particularly difficult.
Transfers are authorized using "private keys"—long strings of characters kept secret. However, this does not fully protect funds from theft.
"Even when you think you are using one of the most robust exchanges in the world, it can still be hacked," Stephane Ifrah, an analyst at Coinhouse, told AFP.
How can hackers still get in?

In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details.
Four new features coming to WhatsApp group chats
WhatsApp this week announced that the filter drawer, which appears when users swipe down on the conversations list, will now include a “Mentions and replies” button alongside other filter options such as Groups, Favorites, Unread and custom filters.
Once tapped, the chat list will show only “unread group conversation[s] where you were either mentioned or received a direct reply, including @all messages,” says WhatsApp.
Additionally, WhatsApp will now let users pin messages indefinitely in group chats, rather than choosing between 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.
Another in-chat feature coming to groups is the ability to “send someone recent messages retroactively after they’ve joined a group just by tapping their name in the chat.” Previously, this was only possible when adding someone to a group, rather than after they had joined.
Finally, WhatsApp is rolling out group status sharing, which lets users post updates visible only to members of a specific group. Other members can view, react to, and add their own statuses, which disappear after 24 hours.

sources.title: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
sources.text:
“I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”
I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh!), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.
By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.
When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.
As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases. I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.
As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.
There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.
“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”
As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)
I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.

sources.text:
اتهم مكتب التحقيقات الاتحادي (إف بي آي) -السبت- كوريا الشمالية بالمسؤولية عن سرقة أكثر من 6 مليارات دولار من الأصول الرقمية من منصة باينانس لتداول العملات المشفرة.
وقال المكتب إن جهات خبيثة من كوريا الشمالية رُصدت وهي تعمل على إخفاء مصدر الأصول المسروقة عبر تحويلها إلى عملة إيثريوم.
أخبار مقترحة
وأضاف أنه يتوقع أن تمر هذه الأصول المسروقة "بمراحل إضافية من غسل الأموال".
ويؤكد المحققون الأميركيون أنهم حددوا هوية الجهة المسؤولة عن عملية السرقة الضخمة هذه، وهي مجموعة من القراصنة الإلكترونيين الكوريين الشماليين تعرف باسم "تريدر ترايتور".
ونشر "إف بي آي" قائمة تضم حوالى 500 عنوان على شبكة "إيثيريوم" يستخدمها أعضاء "تريدر ترايتور" لغسل الأصول المسروقة، وطلب من منصات العملات المشفرة وخدمات التمويل اللامركزي وشركات تحليل "البلوكتشين" حظر المعاملات المرتبطة بهذه العناوين.
ومساء الخميس أعلنت بينانس أنها تعرضت لاختراق أمني قُدرت آثاره المالية بنحو 6.3 مليارات دولار، في واقعة أثارت اضطرابا في سوق الأصول الرقمية، وأعادت المخاوف بشأن قدرة منصات التداول على حماية أموال المستخدمين.
وأعلنت باينانس -إحدى أكبر منصة تداول العملات المشفرة في العالم- ارتفاع نسبة تغطية الخسائر الناجمة عن الهجوم الإلكتروني إلى 90%، بعدما كانت النسبة 80% في تحديثها الأمني السابق، في خطوة تهدف إلى إعادة بناء الاحتياطيات الرقمية المتضررة وحماية أرصدة المستخدمين.
واعتبر مراقبون أن هذا الهجوم ربما يكون الأكبر من نوعه على الإطلاق، متجاوزا في حجمه سرقة 1.5 مليار دولار من منصة "باي بيت" في فبراير/شباط 2025، وهي حادثة نُسبت حينها إلى قراصنة مرتبطين بكوريا الشمالية.

sources.title: واشنطن تحمل كوريا الشمالية مسؤولية "سرقة" 6.3 مليارات دولار
sources.text:
أعلنت منصة "بينانس" لتداول العملات المشفرة، أنها تمكنت من تعويض نسبة 90 بالمئة من الأصول التي سُرقت في اختراق غير مسبوق بلغ حجمه 6.3 مليارات دولار، باستخدام أموال الشركة لشراء رموز رقمية جديدة.
وأكدت منصة "بينانس" أن النسبة المتبقية البالغة 10% تتكون من رموز رقمية أقل سيولة، مما يعني أن استردادها أو شراءها بالكميات المطلوبة قد يستغرق وقتا أطول.
وفي السياق ذاته، أعلن مكتب التحقيقات الاتحادي الأميركي (إف بي آي) أن كوريا الشمالية مسؤولة عن الهجوم السيبراني، منسبا العملية إلى قراصنة ينتمون إلى مجموعة "تريدر ترايتور" المدعومة من الدولة.
وأوضح المكتب أن جهات إنفاذ القانون رصدت عناصر من المجموعة وهم يحولون الأصول المسروقة بشكل أساسي إلى عملة الإيثريوم، مرجحا استخدام خدمات التمويل اللامركزي والتبادل الفوري في عمليات غسيل لاحقة.
وكانت شركة "تي آر إم لابس" لتحليل البلوكتشين قد ربطت الهجوم بالمجموعة ذاتها في وقت سابق، موضحة أن المهاجمين حولوا معظم المبلغ في غضون 20 دقيقة فقط، في محاولة واضحة لتفادي تجميد الأصول.
تفاصيل الاختراق
وقال ريتشارد تنج، الرئيس التنفيذي المشارك للشركة، إن الاختراق كان "هجوما معقدا" تضمن استخدام جهاز كمبيوتر محمول مخترق وبرمجيات خبيثة صممت لحذف الأدلة على نشاطها، مما صعب عمليات التتبع والتحقيق.
وتنوعت الأصول المسروقة بين البتكوين والإيثريوم، بالإضافة إلى عملات مستقرة مثل "تيثر" و"يو إس دي كوين".
وكشف تنج عن أن الشركة خصصت نحو 6.34 مليارات دولار من أموالها لتغطية الخسائر، مؤكدا أن المستخدمين لن يتحملوا الأثر المالي لهذه الواقعة.
وأوضح أن الأموال التي أنفقتها لإعادة شراء الرموز جاءت من استخدام جزء من "صندوق الأصول الآمنة للمستخدمين" البالغة قيمته مليار دولار (وهو احتياطي من البتكوين تحتفظ به لحماية العملاء)، إضافة إلى جزء من صندوق التأمين الخاص بعقودها الآجلة وخزانة الشركة.
وأشارت منصة بينانس إلى أنها أوقفت عمليات سحب أموال العملاء بعد الاختراق، لكنها لا تزال في طريقها لاستئناف السحب غدا الأحد. كما التقطت صورة جديدة للأصول المحتفظ بها على منصتها في إطار عملية "إثبات الاحتياطيات"، مؤكدة أن المستخدمين الذين يحتفظون بالرموز العشرة المدرجة سيتمكنون من التحقق من أن أصولهم مدعومة بنسبة لا تقل عن 1 إلى 1.
وانخفضت أسعارالعملات المشفرة الجمعة، فيما سعت بينانس، أكبر منصة لتداول العملات المشفرة في العالم، إلى طمأنة العملاء بأن أموالهم آمنة. ويرجح أن يكون هذا الهجوم السيبراني أضخم عملية سطو تستهدف منصة لتداول العملات المشفرة حتى الآن.

sources.title: ‘Green Room’ Director Recalls How Patrick Stewart “Saved” Movie From Being Scrapped
sources.text:
Green Room director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to Patrick Stewart ahead of a Los Angeles screening of the film on Friday, recalling how the sci-fi icon “just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us.”
Celebrating the film’s 10th anniversary, Saulnier addressed the crowd and noted Stewart’s death at 86.
“Who’s sad as fuck we lost Patrick Stewart yesterday? Me,” he said in a video posted on the Film Updates X account. “I came here to shamelessly promote Slayground, but instead, I’m just gonna celebrate Patrick Stewart. He had no business doing this movie. He every option to do otherwise.”
Related Stories
The director remembered how production on Green Room was “at the point of no return, building sets, and under the gun without Darcy,” noting that the lead character of Darcy Banker had not yet been cast. However, that’s when the Star Trek star came in.
“We’re fucked, and we were close to shutting down. And Patrick Stewart, out of the blue, sort of expressed interest in the project,” Saulnier said. “And in a whirlwind, about a week later, I was on the phone with him. I left the stage [thinking,] ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’ Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. And the movie was instantly greenlit.”
“We moved forward, and I thank him for just taking that leap and making Green Room a thing,” he added. “Patrick Stewart is why I still can make movies. He saved the day. Too good to be true.”
The Rebel Ridge director remembered Stewart as a “fucking sweetheart, true gentleman, [who was a] very kind leader to our whole cast.” He also shared a story about how one day, the actor came to him and said he “wanted to add a little something” to a scene.
“I was like, ‘What is it, Patrick?’ He’s like, ‘Well, during this one part of the scene, when the camera’s coming through there, I’d like to say, fuck!’ And I was like, ‘And?’ ‘Just fuck.’ I was like. ‘Permission granted, sir,’” Saulnier recounted. “And I just knew that he was completely aligned with the film, its aesthetic, its intentions and with me as a filmmaker, and it was just this lovely, lovely thing.”
Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak announced. After his death, his former co-stars and Hollywood notables shared an outpouring of tributes.
Among those who have paid homage to the X-Men star are Ian McKellen, Kevin Feige, William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane, Hugh Jackman, Minnie Driver, Rebecca Romijn, Halle Berry and James Marsden, among many others.

sources.text:
Lawson disqualified from Mexico City GP Qualifying for technical breach
Liam Lawson's eventful weekend at the Mexico City Grand Prix has continued with his disqualification from Saturday's Qualifying hour.
Liam Lawson has been disqualified from Qualifying for the Mexico City Grand Prix following a technical breach on his Racing Bulls challenger.
The New Zealander had qualified an impressive eighth ahead of his team mate Arvid Lindblad in the closely-fought session, but was due to lose a position after he received a one-place grid penalty for an earlier incident with Red Bull's Max Verstappen in FP2.
While that would've left him to start the race from P9, Lawson was referred to the stewards after it was noted that he was "in breach of the minimum MGU-K power requirement just after crossing the line on his fastest lap in Q2".
The FIA Technical Delegate's report added: "The driver maximum power demand and the electrical DC power of the ERS-K were reduced at greater rates than what is permitted by the Regulations."
Lawson was therefore summoned after Qualifying and it was determined that the infringement warranted disqualification, which means that he is due to start the race from the back of the grid.
The stewards heard from Racing Bulls' representatives, Lawson, the Single Seater Sporting Director and members of the FIA Technical team, including the FIA Technical Delegate.
"Evidence submitted, which was accepted by all parties present, showed that after the control line at the end of his fastest lap in Q2, the driver did not lift off the power immediately," read the stewards’ decision document. "This resulted in the rate of reduction of MGU-K deployment required to achieve the regulated 'step down', not being achieved.
"The team argued that this did not provide any performance advantage however it is clear that non-compliance with the Technical Regulations is not excused if no performance advantage is gained. Further, these regulations require that a car must comply with them at all times during an event.
"The stewards note in particular that the team self-disclosed the breach however there are a multitude of precedents that require us, despite all mitigating circumstances, to impose a penalty of disqualfication where a car does not comply with the Technical Regulations."

sources.text:
EA recently announced it was shutting down BioWare, ending a studio responsible for multiple hit games over 30 years. According to a new report, EA's decision was driven by economics, as it had to choose between funding a new Mass Effect and backing the safer bet, Star Wars: Battlefront 3.
Bloomberg's Jason Schreier reported that EA had to choose between two costly projects, and with the added pressure of paying off $18 billion in leveraged debt after its sale to a business consortium and Saudi Arabia's investment fund, Battlefront 3 made more financial sense. To add insult to injury, Battlefront 3 isn't even in development yet, and it hasn't been officially announced.
"They chose to invest in Star Wars and shut down BioWare as a result, said the people familiar, speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to talk to the press," Schreier wrote. "Star Wars: Battlefront 3 has not even begun development yet, but EA executives saw it as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect--and the publisher behind Battlefield has always been more comfortable with shooters than RPGs."
Schreier added that "corporate politics" may have also influenced the decision, as one of the studio's key advocates, senior EA exec Laura Miele, was reportedly sidelined when EA Sports veterans David Tinson and Cam Weber were promoted. BioWare also experienced several flops over the last decade, with Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to meet sales expectations, which further influenced EA's decision to shut down the studio.
After BioWare's closure, more details on its Mass Effect project have emerged. A trailer for Mass Effect: Universe was posted online last week; the game's details made it sound like a sci-fi version of John Wick, and video game composer Austin Wintory shared an experimental score as part of his Mass Effect audition tape.

sources.title: Anthropic: That Claude Code extension compromise… couldn't be us
sources.text:
Anthropic has denied allegations that a malicious version of the official Claude Code extension published to Cursor’s marketplace was linked to any kind of compromise of its own systems.
The company was forced to issue a statement after prominent figures in the cybersecurity industry alleged that the extension, which infected up to 5,000 developers, was uploaded to Cursor’s marketplace following a breach at Claudemaker Towers.
Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic’s technical staff, Xeeted today: "We're working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic's systems or employee laptops.
"A malicious actor used access to Cursor's marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn't build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected, and this only impacts Cursor users."
First spotted by EDR vendor Phorion, an unknown party pushed an update to Cursor's official Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code that contained a persistent SSH backdoor written for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
According to Cursor, the extension – version 2.1.313 – was available to download for around 11 hours between 0227 and 1335 PT (0927 and 2035 UTC) on Thursday.
The vendors' analyses of the implant revealed that it collected information about the host machine and user, including usernames, configured Git emails, and public IP addresses, as well as attempting to open a reverse SSH tunnel.
Crucially, Cursor echoed Phorion's assessment that the package contained a critical flaw.
The script responsible for opening the SSH tunnel required admin rights on macOS and Windows to do so, and in the vast majority of cases it did not have these, resulting in failure.
Regardless, the extension still forwards the collected host and user data to the attacker, as well as dropping the attacker's SSH key and installing the persistence mechanism, so developers must go threat hunting in case their instance allows for the SSH tunnel to be created successfully.
Simply installing the latest version of the extension is not enough to clear the persistence mechanism, either.
The full details of how to remediate the issue, and links to download scripts to wipe the infection, are laid out in Cursor's account of the situation.
Aside from Rieseberg's statement today, neither Cursor nor Anthropic have commented on how the malicious package made its way to the official marketplace.
Anthropic's position is that a malicious actor uploaded the tampered copy to Cursor, but the latter has not outlined how it reached the marketpplace.
"[We] removed the malicious version from the marketplace immediately upon detection and blocked further distribution," Cursor said in the advisory. "We followed with a full shutdown of the VSCode Marketplace out of an abundance of caution."
It also ran checks to confirm no other extensions were compromised in the same way, rotated its own keys before restoring the marketplace, and worked with a cloud hosting provider to block the connection to the attacker's server, it said. ®

sources.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
sources.text:
An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.
The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.
“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here.

Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Some traders on social media are dubbing the sell-off “Bloody Friday.”
Preelection jitters could also be playing a role, as “cold runs” have typically preceded midterm contests, as noted by wealth manager Stephen Rohrer at Life Financial Group.

sources.title: Binance Hack Shows Why Offshore Exchanges Need US Oversight, CFTC Chair Says
sources.text:
In brief
- CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC the $6.4 billion Binance hack “proves our exact point” for the crypto-market rules the agency proposed this month.
- Selig characterized the attack as a laptop-introduced vulnerability rather than a blockchain flaw—but Binance has since found “additional points of breach.”
- The CFTC chair cast on-chain traceability as a regulatory advantage.
The record-breaking hack of Binance is exactly why offshore crypto exchanges need U.S. oversight, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig argued, using the roughly $6.4 billion theft to press the agency’s case for a federal rulebook.
Speaking to CNBC on Friday, Selig said the breach “proves our exact point” behind the crypto-market regulations the agency proposed earlier this month.
“The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don’t have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States,” he said, pitching a “federal option” that would let such venues register with the CFTC and submit to the same cybersecurity standards that govern U.S. markets.
Selig sought to downplay the role of blockchain itself in the attack. The exploit, he said, didn’t break the underlying blockchain, in this case Ethereum, or its smart contracts, but exploited a vulnerability he believed was “introduced from someone’s laptop,” the kind of incident that happens in traditional markets too.
The difference with crypto, he said, is speed: funds can move far faster, and attackers can route them through tools like Tornado Cash to obscure their trail.
Selig’s characterization, though, may be incomplete. Binance initially pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, but said Friday that its investigation had since uncovered “additional points of breach,” with CEO Richard Teng calling it “a more complex attack process” that “did not simply use one engineer’s permissions.”
And while the theft did not expose a flaw in Ethereum itself, the attack did play out partly on-chain: The attacker used EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature that lets ordinary wallets run smart-contract code, to turn a Binance hot wallet into a “sweeper” using 50 pre-signed authorizations, draining its assets.
TRM Labs said the broader breach points to a compromise of Binance’s signing infrastructure rather than a weakness in any blockchain.
Selig framed the blockchain’s transparency as a regulatory advantage regardless. “The fact that we can trace transactions on-chain, even when some of these technologies are used to obfuscate that, gives regulators a lot of potential to be really cop on the beat here,” he said.
The comments sharpen a pitch Selig has been making for weeks. The CFTC has pressed ahead with its own crypto rulemaking rather than wait on Congress, sending the White House proposals that would define event contracts as “swaps” and floating a plan to bring crypto exchanges under federal oversight, part of a broader shift in which regulators have taken the lead after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.
The Binance hack hands that effort a vivid talking point.The exploit is the largest in crypto history, with Binance setting aside $6.34 billion to cover losses and assuring users their assets are safe. The Secret Service and FBI have opened a probe, and TRM Labs and Chainalysis have tied the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group.

sources.text:
The United States government’s response to escalating cyberscams is fragmented, leaving victims with limited options to recover lost funds, according to an investigation conducted by Democrats on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee (JEC).
The investigation, led by Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, found that federal agencies do not have a consolidated or comprehensive record of how much money has been lost to cyberfraud, how much has been seized from overseas scam compounds, or how much has been returned to victims.
The report, published Tuesday, also concludes that the government does not “incentivize” private sector actors—such as financial institutions and social media companies—to “proactively detect and address abuse of the services that they provide while also protecting user privacy.”
Online scam operations are not new, and neither is the knowledge that the issue is escalating. The FBI released an April report showing that Americans lost nearly $18 billion in 2025, amounting to more than $2 million an hour. Overall reported internet-crime losses—a broader category—reached $20.9 billion, up 26% from 2024 and roughly triple the 2021 total.
While the problem grows worse, the response to these crimes has not scaled along with it. The Congressional investigation demonstrates that only a fraction of the money lost to scams is recovered. It also points to the fact that the government fails to fully report on its existing repatriation measures.
The FBI told the committee that it returned $336 million to scam victims in 2025, and the Secret Service returned more than $770 million in seized assets to fraud victims in fiscal years 2024 and 2025—though that money had come from a range of fraud schemes, not just cyber threats.
Suzanne Sando, a fraud analyst at Javelin Strategy & Research, points out that “fragmentation” in the reporting system—including the differing time periods and fraud categories demonstrated above—complicates the government’s ability to grasp the full extent of the problem.
“Many of the groups and entities that scam victims report their losses to operate on disparate systems,” Sando says. “The fragmented nature of these reporting entities means there’s a lack of true accounting of losses—which also means that our grasp of overall scam losses is likely less than the truth of the situation.”
The Congressional report calls on the federal government to enact new legislation to address the rising issue, including the ReportScams.Gov Act, a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by Hassan and Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott “to mandate a unified federal strategy to combat scams and establish a central location for Americans to find information and assistance regarding scams.”
A more coordinated reporting system could help researchers and advocates better assess the scale of the problem. Another benefit would be helping the public stay informed about potential schemes, allowing advocacy groups to develop preventive strategies and educational materials for at-risk populations, like senior citizens and minors.

Individuals under 18 reported nearly $13 million in losses across 13,168 internet-crime complaints in 2025, according to the same report.

sources.title: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth
sources.text:
Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite.
The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you."
Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit.
"During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post.
And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink:
Blue marble below,
Data streams in silent grace,
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.
Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku.
According to Google's calculations, if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year).
Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening.
After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation.
Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam.
The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si).
"For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month.
"While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study."
Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®

sources.text:
واصل الدولي المغربي عبد الرزاق حمد الله تعزيز سجله التهديفي في الدوري السعودي، بعدما وقع على هدف التعاون الوحيد أمام الاتفاق، في المباراة التي انتهت بالتعادل بهدف لمثله، ضمن الجولة الثانية عشرة من منافسات دوري روشن.
وكان المهاجم المغربي وراء تقدم التعاون في المواجهة، بعدما نجح في تحويل ركلة جزاء إلى هدف عند الدقيقة الـ26، مؤكداً مجدداً حسه التهديفي وقدرته على صناعة الفارق، رغم الوضعية الصعبة التي يمر منها فريقه في المسابقة.
ومنح هذا الهدف حمد الله فرصة جديدة لتعزيز أرقامه التاريخية، إذ رفع مجموع مساهماته التهديفية في دوري روشن إلى 185 مساهمة، ليواصل تصدر قائمة أكثر اللاعبين مساهمة في الأهداف بتاريخ المسابقة.
كما بات المهاجم المغربي على بعد هدف واحد من معادلة الرقم القياسي لأفضل هداف في تاريخ الدوري السعودي للمحترفين، والذي يحمله السوري عمر السومة برصيد 161 هدفاً، مقابل 160 هدفاً في رصيد حمد الله، في انتظار ما ستسفر عنه المباريات المقبلة.
وعلى المستوى الجماعي، لم يكن هدف حمد الله كافياً لمنح التعاون انتصاره الأول هذا الموسم، بعدما تمكن عبد الله الخطيب من تعديل النتيجة للاتفاق في الدقيقة الـ90، ليضيع الفريق المضيف نقطتين جديدتين في الأمتار الأخيرة من اللقاء.

clusters.title_hint: Electronic health record phenotype choice and real-world outcome estimates: A propensity score–matched comparison of three invasive breast cancer definitions in TriNetX

sources.title: Electronic health record phenotype choice and real-world outcome estimates: A propensity score–matched comparison of three invasive breast cancer definitions in TriNetX
sources.text:
by Jui-Kun Chiang, Po-Chen Chiang, Malcolm Koo
Electronic health record-based oncology studies depend on computable case definitions, but different operational definitions may identify different patient populations and change downstream estimates. This retrospective benchmarking cohort study evaluated three definitions of incident invasive breast cancer in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network: at least one malignant breast cancer diagnosis code (Dx1), a repeated diagnosis-code definition within 90 days (Dx2), and a diagnosis code plus breast cancer-directed treatment evidence (DxTx). Female patients aged 20 years or older were identified after a 12-month washout period and exclusion of patients with carcinoma in situ only. Pairwise one-to-one propensity-score matching was performed using 13 baseline covariates. Outcomes were all-cause mortality and time to the first emergency department visits, assessed from day 180 after the index date to 1, 3, and 5 years after the original index date. Appendicitis and femoral neck fracture were included as negative-control outcomes. Dx1, Dx2, and DxTx identified 1,450,233, 678,739, and 578,576 patients, respectively. After matching, more restrictive definitions were consistently associated with higher hazards of mortality and emergency department visits. For mortality, hazard ratios ranged from 1.26 to 1.32 for DxTx versus Dx1, 1.13 to 1.14 for Dx2 versus Dx1, and 1.13 to 1.17 for DxTx versus Dx2 across assessment windows. Emergency department visit estimates showed a similar but attenuating pattern. These associations should be interpreted as differences between phenotype-defined populations arising from selection and ascertainment mechanisms rather than as treatment effects. Negative-control outcomes were generally close to the null; small appendicitis associations observed in comparisons involving Dx1 did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings indicate that plausible electronic health record-based breast cancer definitions are not analytically interchangeable. Phenotype specification should therefore be treated as a core analytic decision and evaluated through transparent reporting and sensitivity analyses.

sources.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
sources.text:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.
Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.
Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.
The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.
“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”
Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.
At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI, a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther, a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS.
Nexus, a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.
Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.
The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula.
Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.
Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science.

clusters.title_hint: Input Lag Is So Bad in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Nintendo Switch 2 That Players Suffer From a 'Competitive Disadvantage'

sources.title: Input Lag Is So Bad in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Nintendo Switch 2 That Players Suffer From a 'Competitive Disadvantage'
sources.text:
If you’re playing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Nintendo Switch 2, beware: you’re at a disadvantage in competitive Multiplayer due to crushing input lag that is much worse than the other platforms.
Digital Foundry’s analysis of the performance of the Switch 2 version of Modern Warfare 4 — the first Call of Duty released on a Nintendo console since 2013’s Ghosts — found that the input lag on Switch 2 can be two times longer than on PS5 at 60fps.
In competitive Multiplayer, Switch 2 aims for 60fps and, according to DF, hits that target most of the time (although some things do cause the frame rate to drop, including looking through the transparent visor of a riot shield).
Call of Duty Multiplayer prides itself on rock solid 60fps gameplay, which provides a smooth, responsive experience for those who fuss over their K/D ratio in, for example, 6v6. It’s crucial that all platforms the game is available on offer at least 60fps to provide a level playing field for Multiplayer fans — although the debate about the advantage PC players have over console has dogged Call of Duty since the dawn of crossplay.
DF reports that Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) support “helps smooth out” framerate drops on supported displays, although you’ll have a harder time of it in terms of performance playing through portable mode.
And then we come to responsiveness. DF’s tests show 81ms in docked mode and 100ms in portable mode, the latter of which is double the PS5’s 49.1. In fact, DF found that Multiplayer in portable mode ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst. DF called this "actually deleterious to performance.”
DF seems generally happy with the Switch 2 version, which was handled by port specialist Digital Legends with support from Infinity Ward. But if you’re into Multiplayer, the inescapable fact is you are at a disadvantage. No matter how fast your trigger finger, the Switch 2 will take longer to respond.
Outside of Multiplayer it’s a different story. The Campaign runs at 30fps, which was good enough for IGN’s Simon Cardy when he played the Switch 2 version of Modern Warfare 4.
“Granted, the textures are nowhere near as detailed, with flat surfaces and faces smoothed over to give the impression of plasticine versions of the campaign’s characters,” he said. “It's by no means a looker, but considering the reduced horsepower Nintendo’s latest console is working with, the gameplay itself was smooth, running at 30fps at 4K while docked.”
“Yes, it's quite a visual downgrade when compared to the likes of PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X, but that comes with the territory,” he continued. “And if you’re solely a Nintendo owner who’s been locked out of Call of Duty for over a decade, you’re getting a version of Modern Warfare 4 that feels every bit as snappy as the series usually is, even if it’s a bit muddier than Nintendo’s own crisp visuals.”
Why is Call of Duty releasing on a Nintendo console now, 14 years after the last time? It has to do with Microsoft’s $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard. Back when Microsoft was facing regulatory hurdles, one announcement designed to help convince the powers that be to green light the buyout was a 10-year commitment to bring Call of Duty to Nintendo following the merger.
“Microsoft is committed to helping bring more games to more people — however they choose to play,” then Xbox boss Phil Spencer said in December 2022. Four years later, and with the Activision Blizzard buyout done and dusted, Call of Duty is on Switch
