sources.text:
Verstappen reveals what 'killed my lap' as he assesses Red Bull's Mexico City GP Qualifying performance
Max Verstappen looked like challenging for pole position ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix before an error on his final attempt.
Max Verstappen has detailed what "killed his lap" in Qualifying for the Mexico City Grand Prix, with the Red Bull driver ultimately set to start P5 for Sunday's race.
The four-time World Champion featured towards the front in Saturday's Qualifying session and sat second after the opening runs in Q3 at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.
But whereas others improved with their second attempts, Verstappen failed to go quicker after running deep at the Turn 13 hairpin through the stadium section having just passed Lando Norris' McLaren.
It left Verstappen fourth, with the Dutchman set to start fifth after earning himself a one-place grid penalty for a practice collision with Liam Lawson on Friday.
"Already going into Turn 12 I had a car very close to me, so I already lost time there with the dirty air," said Verstappen.
"Then going into the hairpin, instead of going on the left, I had one car on my right where you normally want to open up the corner.
"It's a bit of an awkward angle then how you have to go into the hairpin, plus you lose your reference on the right hand side where you are constantly looking, because it's a difficult corner to get right.
"That then killed my lap but I think for me the most promising thing is of course how we turned it around because in practice I was not very happy. Qualifying was good, we were fighting for pole for sure."
Red Bull team mate Isack Hadjar will start from P7, despite the Frenchman having a difficult session, particularly with the brakes.
"I just don't know how to drive it. It's fast, it's just not really drivable and I just sucked really," said Hadjar.
"Very [frustrating] because the car is as competitive as the last couple of weekends and we produce a lap worthy of P-nowhere. To be P7, I'm lucky."

sources.title: NASA ponders a Hubble servicing mission or a controlled deorbit
sources.text:
NASA has posted a contract opportunity notice, also known as a request for information, from commercial space orgs who can service the Hubble Space Telescope.
Hubble was always looked after by NASA astronauts flying on the Space Shuttle, yet the last Hubble Space Telescope (HST) servicing mission was the STS-125 Space Shuttle flight, launched on May 11, 2009. At the time, scientists hoped the mission would add another five years of operational life to the venerable spacecraft. Almost 17 years on, the HST (aka Hubble) is still delivering science.
However, time is running out for the observatory. NASA reckons there is a 10 percent chance it could reenter the Earth's atmosphere by September 2032, rising to 50 percent by December 2033. As the end of the Swift mission showed, increased solar activity can cause greater-than-anticipated atmospheric drag.
Also, like Swift, Hubble has no propulsion system, and so when it reenters (as it will, without intervention), the reentry will be uncontrolled. Hubble is sufficiently massive that there is a remote chance somebody on the ground could have a very bad day when that happens.
As such, one mission option suggested by NASA is a vehicle to grapple the observatory and perform a controlled reentry and disposal.
However, there are other options. Something to boost the telescope's orbit up to at least 600 km, or another to "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience and expected on-orbit lifetime."
Both are intriguing options, and important since, as NASA acknowledges, no replacement for Hubble is expected before the 2040s, when the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) could become operational. Despite the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, Hubble remains in high demand, with NASA reporting a 7:1 oversubscription.
Before becoming NASA Administrator, Jared Isaacman advocated a SpaceX mission to boost the Hubble, but the idea was ultimately rejected. Similar plans could now be dusted off. NASA's requirement is for a mission to occur by 2032, and not harm the Hubble.
A soft-capture mechanism was fitted to Hubble during the STS-125 mission, which will mean docking with the spacecraft will be easier than the grappling planned for Swift. Then, the question is what to do with it. A controlled reentry is one option. The other options – boosting to a higher altitude or "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience" are intriguing. Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV), for example, is capable of on-orbit servicing and extending the lifetime of satellites. The Hubble is an order of magnitude more challenging, but the technological hurdles can be overcome with time and funding.
Last year, The Register spoke with Dr John Grunsfeld, one of the astronauts (now retired) who worked on Hubble during the STS-125 mission. Grunsfeld told us that the veteran spacecraft faced death by a thousand cuts as its budget was whittled away. The observatory itself recently switched from three to one gyro mode (the telescope uses gyros to control where it is pointed) to eke out a few more years of operational life.
At this point, NASA is looking for information and comment – this isn't a request for proposals. There is no indication of how much the agency expects to pay. However, the timescale is immutable. Without intervention, Hubble will make an uncontrolled reentry in the coming years. ®

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.
The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:
Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.
Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.
A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.
A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.
Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

sources.title: A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy
sources.text: You might imagine space to be empty. But the seeming void contains a barely perceptible fog of hydrogen and other neutral atoms. In 2020, NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft, having passed the orbit of Pluto, measured a proxy for the amount of hydrogen around it. In the area between stars in our galaxy — the “interstellar medium,” or ISM — New Horizons found around 130 hydrogen atoms per liter of space.

sources.title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated
sources.text:
A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.
The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.
"What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. "What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s."

clusters.title_hint: World’s tallest Day of the Dead sculpture erected in Mexico City

sources.title: World’s tallest Day of the Dead sculpture erected in Mexico City
sources.text:
Mexico City has broken a Guinness World Record during its preparations for this year’s Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos) celebrations. At nearly 110 feet tall, the colorful sculpture of a female skeleton currently standing in the capital city’s town square (the Zócalo) is officially the world’s tallest La Catrina monument. The roughly 11-story project made from steel and fiberglass required about 140 people to assemble, and overshadows the town of Puerto Vallarta’s 92.3-foot Catrina built back in 2023. The height isn’t the only impressive aspect, either. Her purple dress measures over 88 feet long, while the memorial altar (called an ofrenda) is surrounded by an estimated 70,00 marigold plants grown in the nearby Xochimilco borough.
Observed each year on November 1 and 2, Mexico’s Day of the Dead is famously dedicated to celebrating and honoring deceased family members and loved ones. Historians are divided on its exact origins—while some researchers contend it possesses genuine Indigenous pre-Hispanic roots, others argue the holiday is a more recent rebrand of Spanish traditions intended to promote cultural pride. Regardless of the answer, Day of the Dead has evolved into one of the country’s most popular and iconic observances. Every year, celebrants often wear skeleton-themed costumes and construct ofrendas, while families and friends gather to fondly recall the departed.
Apart from its size, Mexico City’s record-breaking sculpture is a relatively traditional example of La Catrina, one of Day of the Dead’s most recognizable figures. It’s also much easier to trace La Catrina’s history compared to the holiday’s origins. The figure is based on early 20th century Mexican illustrator José Guadalupe Posada’s most famous work, “La Calavera Catrina” ( or “The Elegant Skull”). Posada’s illustration was released posthumously, and depicts a woman’s skeleton dressed in stylish clothing. Art historians widely view “La Calavera Catrina” as a critique of upper-class Mexican women who attempted to mirror European fashions of the era. Posada’s piece was later expanded upon by the muralist Diego Rivera in 1946-1947.
Similarly inspired iconography has since become a mainstay of Day of the Dead celebrations. La Catrina sculptures like the new record breaker in Mexico City are frequently surrounded by marigolds. Also known as cempasúchil, the flowers are traditionally believed to help guide spirits home with their scent and colorful petals.
Like life itself, Mexico City’s building-sized La Catrina is only temporary. Admirers will be able to visit the installation and its altar only until November 2.

with Knowledge Graphs: A Production

sources.title:
How to Detect Financial Fraud Patterns
with Knowledge Graphs: A Production
Guide
sources.text:
Most anti-fraud architectures in enterprise payment workflows evaluate transactions in isolation.
When an invoice arrives, an automated rules engine checks it against static thresholds. It checks whether the dollar amount falls within normal limits, whether the vendor is on an approved vendor list, and whether the submitting IP address looks familiar. If the individual attributes look plausible, the payment clears.
The problem with this approach is structural. Sophisticated fraud schemes like money mule rings, circular invoicing loops, and vendor collision rarely produce transactions that alert individual thresholds. A shell company invoicing $4,800 to stay under a $5,000 dual sign-off threshold looks completely fine in isolation. But when 25 seemingly independent vendors all route disbursements to the same bank account, the coordinated pattern starts to become clear.
You won't find the warning in the attributes of an isolated transaction. It lives in the topology of the payment network.
In a relational database, tracing these multi-entity relationships requires recursive cell joins across tables of vendors, invoices, payments, and bank accounts. But as tables grow into millions of rows, deep path traversals quickly degrade query performance. Graph databases solve this by storing relationships as first-class, index-free adjacency pointers, turning multi-hop traversals into constant-time lookups.
In this tutorial, you'll explore the architecture of an end-to-end relational fraud detection pipeline built on Neo4j. You'll see how to model financial entities as a graph, precompute derived edges to optimize query latency, and write parameterized Cypher queries to uncover five core procurement fraud schemes.
The complete reference implementation is available in the fraud-detection-knowledge-graphs repository.
In accounts payable pipelines, risk checks typically operate on isolated records:
# Transaction-level view — nothing suspicious
transactions = [
{"vendor": "Alpha Corp", "amount": 5200.00, "date": "2025-08-01"},
{"vendor": "Beta LLC", "amount": 4800.00, "date": "2025-08-02"},
{"vendor": "Gamma Inc", "amount": 5100.00, "date": "2025-08-03"},
]
# All amounts within normal range ($1K–$15K). All vendors valid.
# Dates are sequential. Nothing triggers any rule.
When you map those same records to an interconnected graph, the hidden structure becomes clear right away:
# Graph view — all three vendors pay to the same account
connections = {
"ACC-MULE-001": ["Alpha Corp", "Beta LLC", "Gamma Inc"],
"ACC-0042": ["Delta Corp", "Epsilon LLC"],
"ACC-0099": ["Zeta GmbH"],
}
# ACC-MULE-001 receives from 25+ vendors. That's a money mule ring.
# The convergence is the red flag.
The underlying data hasn't changed. But when you evaluate transactions within an entity graph, the coordinated funnel stands out.
In a relational database, connecting these dots requires multiple joins across separate table. In a knowledge graph, the connections are stored directly as edges connecting nodes, which allows you to query them in a single traversal.

| Circular Rings | Vendors invoicing each other in a closed loop | Each invoice looks legitimate alone |
| Money Mule Rings | Many vendors funneling to one controlled account | No single payment is anomalous |
